expectations.text: The reply opens with a recommendation against a fixed quota of low ratings and says why (it labels a fixed share of every team whatever its actual performance), while taking the CEO's underlying concern seriously.
expectations.evidence: Opens: "Run this year's reviews as an honest, calibrated process... Leave out the 10% quota and the automatic exit." Why: "A quota would give you about 120 names, and in court each one needs evidence that a ranking can't supply"; process table: "A quota produces a bottom group whether or not anyone is underperforming." CEO concern: "He may well be right that ratings are inflated, and the design treats that as the problem"; 'What your CEO still gets' list.

expectations.text: The reply cites at least one real piece of evidence on forced or stack ranking, or on what drives performance differences between teams, with its source (for example Microsoft dropping stack ranking in 2013, simulation research on forced distribution, or research on managers' effect on teams).
expectations.evidence: "Simulated gains come mostly in the first years and depend on reliable ratings (Scullen et al., 2005)" with Wiley link; "Microsoft dropped stack ranking in 2013 because it worked against teamwork (SHRM)"; process design adds Trevor & Nyberg 2008 on survivor turnover and BAG 2 AZR 667/02.

expectations.text: The reply flags that the works council must consent to the appraisal system in both countries (Netherlands: article 27(1)(g) WOR or its consent right on staff appraisal; Germany: §94 BetrVG appraisal principles), and that a plan starting from a ranking is weak ground for a later dismissal (the Dutch court expects timely notice, support and a real chance to improve; in Germany a low-performance dismissal usually needs a warning and proof).
expectations.evidence: "In both offices the works council has to consent to the rating system (art. 27(1)(g) WOR; §94 BetrVG)"; process table: NL cantonal court asks whether the person "was told in good time and given a real chance to improve... (art. 7:669(3)(d) BW). A plan that starts from a ranking doesn't meet that test"; DE: "The employer has to show a clear, long-term shortfall... Usually a written warning (Abmahnung) and a further period first."

expectations.text: The reply delivers a usable alternative process: clear expectations per role, calibration that aligns standards and checks for bias without forcing a distribution, and individual handling of real underperformance with support and a realistic period.
expectations.evidence: Written expectations per role and level; calibration "The purpose is to align standards across managers, test the evidence and check for bias. There is no target distribution"; HRBP checks clarity, workload, tools and the manager's part before a plan; "90 days by default. 60 days only where the gap is narrow and was clearly raised before this cycle; up to 120 days for complex roles", fortnightly check-ins, open outcomes.

expectations.text: The reply includes a check of ratings by group (such as gender, age, part-time or people on leave) before ratings are used for pay, plans or exits.
expectations.evidence: Process 6.6: "Before ratings are final, HR compares the share of each rating by gender, age (50 and over), part-time status, recent leave, location, and nationality where that is lawful... the department head and HR business partner review those cases before ratings go final." The manager briefing repeats it.

expectations.text: The reply gives the user a line or approach for a private conversation with the CEO first, and a usable manager briefing or its outline.
expectations.evidence: "First step: talk to him privately this week, before anything reaches managers or the works councils. A line you can use: 'You're right that we carry underperformance nobody names...'" manager-briefing.md is complete, with dates, evidence rules, scripts, plan form and FAQ.

overall_quality.evidence: A tight, honest reply with a good private CEO line, backed by an accurate process paper (legal table, equality check, dignity at exit, cost separation) and a practical briefing.

factual_errors.evidence: Checked art. 27(1)(e)/(g) and 27(5) WOR, 7:669(3)(d), 7:670, 7:670b BW, §94(2)/§102 BetrVG, BAG 11 Dec 2003, §159 SGB III 12-week Sperrzeit, §167(2)/§168 SGB IX, Trevor & Nyberg 1%→31%, cost arithmetic (60 x €65k x 0.5-2 ≈ €2-8M): correct. Minor: the court's check that a dissolution isn't linked to illness is in 7:671b BW rather than 7:670, which is not material.

skill_leak.evidence: No mention of a skill or reference files.

owns_result.evidence: The prompt is a proposed policy, not a bad outcome.

best_insight.value: Keep the appraisal system the works councils have already agreed and sharpen guidance and calibration within it, the fastest lawful route this cycle; a quota-driven exit programme may anyway count as dismissals for reasons not related to the individual.

suggestions.assertion: The reply delivers a usable alternative process: clear expectations per role, calibration that aligns standards and checks for bias without forcing a distribution, and individual handling of real underperformance with support and a realistic period.
suggestions.reason: Several samples swap the quota for a company- or function-level 'expected range' (e.g. 10-17% at the bottom) drawn from an unsourced framework. Add a check that no expected or target share is introduced, or that any reference range is sourced and never used to move a rating.

suggestions.assertion: The reply gives the user a line or approach for a private conversation with the CEO first, and a usable manager briefing or its outline.
suggestions.reason: Nearly any CEO talking point passes. Consider requiring that the conversation comes before ExCo, managers or works councils and that it tests what 'it worked at his last company' meant (measure, period, legal setting).

No assertion checks that the reply separates a possible cost or headcount goal from performance management (restructuring route, collective-dismissal rules if exits are driven by a fixed number). The strongest samples do this.
No assertion checks the Dutch route for a performance dismissal (cantonal court, not UWV); at least one sample gets this wrong and still passes assertion 3.

eval_feedback.overall: Passes all six with clear evidence; the shared suggestions on assertions 4 and 6 still apply.
